en: The Philippine eagle, our national bird, uses its dark brown crest feathers to camouflage itself in the rainforest canopy.
The narra, our national tree, sheds its leaves during the dry season to conserve water and produces hard, durable wood.
Ifugao farmers use stone walls and gravity-fed irrigation to channel mountain spring water through their cascading rice terraces.
During the nesting season, female Pawikan sea turtles crawl onto Philippine beaches to lay their eggs in the sand.
The Tubbataha Reef Natural Park is a protected marine sanctuary featuring massive coral atolls teeming with diverse fish species.
Our national flower, the sampaguita, releases its strongest sweet fragrance at night to attract pollinating moths.
The carabao, our national animal, rolls in mud to cool its body and protect its skin from insects.
The waling-waling orchid is an epiphyte that uses its aerial roots to absorb moisture directly from the humid air.
Our national fish, the bangus, can survive in both saltwater and freshwater because it adapts its internal salt balance.
Abaca plants produce exceptionally strong leaf fibers that indigenous weavers use to craft durable ropes and traditional textiles.
Fireflies, locally called kuliglig, produce cold light through a chemical reaction in their abdomens to attract mates in the dark.
The Philippine tarsier has enormous eyes that gather maximum light, allowing this tiny nocturnal primate to hunt insects in total darkness.
